analysis_steps.goal: Compute mass flow rates, momenta, momentum fluxes, kinetic energy fluxes, and lifting factors

method.value: Compute mass flow rate as M_flow / (R / v), flow momentum as M_flow * v, momentum flux as M_dot * v, kinetic energy flux as 0.5 * M_dot * v^2, and lifting factor as M_flow * R_flow / P_drive; compare with AGN radiative luminosity (L_AGN = 10 * L_nuc) and X-ray cavity mechanical power.

evidence.quote: The flow momentum flux is calculated as $\dot{M} v$, where $\dot{M}$ is the mass flow rate in gm s$^{-1}$ and $v$ is the flow speed in cm s$^{-1}$. $\dot{M}$ is estimated by dividing the mass of the flow by the time it takes the flow to reach its projected size ($R/v$).
We define the molecular flow kinetic energy flux as 0.5$\dot{M} v^2$, where $\dot{M}$ is the mass flow rate and $v$ is the average speed of the flow.
This phenomenon is explored further in Figure [2](#thrust), where we compare the product of the mass and flow size per unit power. We refer to this as the lifting factor.

findings_qualitative.value: Thirty to seventy percent of the molecular gas in BCGs lies outside the nucleus in extended filamentary flows, compared to 3-10 percent in AGN, composite, and starburst galaxies.

evidence.quote: Thirty to seventy percent of the gas lies outside of the nucleus in extended, filamentary structures that appear to be moving relative to the BCG.
In AGN hosting galaxies the amount of molecular gas in the outflow is only $\sim$10 percent. It is even lower in composite and starburst galaxies at $\sim$3 percent.

findings_qualitative.value: Radio-mode feedback in BCGs yields lifting factors (M_flow * R_flow / P_drive) that exceed starbursts and quasar nuclei by two to three orders of magnitude.

evidence.quote: The product of the molecular gas mass and lifting altitude divided by the AGN or starburst power — a parameter referred to as the lifting factor—exceeds starbursts and quasar nuclei by two to three orders of magnitude, respectively.

findings_qualitative.value: The kinetic energy flux of molecular gas flows generally lies near or below a few percent of the AGN or starburst driving power across all galaxy types.

evidence.quote: Figure [1](#power) shows that the kinetic energy fluxes of molecular gas in most systems lie near or below a few percent of the AGN or starburst power.

findings_qualitative.value: Escaped molecular gas fractions in BCGs are negligible, indicating a molecular fountain where lifted gas eventually returns to the galaxy.

evidence.quote: We found that for all BCGs the escaped gas fraction is negligible.
Radio-mechanical feedback is likely driving a fountain of hot and cold gas that eventually returns to the central galaxy.

claims.hypothesis: Radio-mechanical feedback in BCGs is more effective at lifting large masses of molecular gas to high altitudes per unit driving power than quasar winds or starbursts.
claims.experiment: Measure molecular flow masses, projected sizes, and velocities from spatially resolved CO observations of 14 BCGs, compute the lifting factor (M_flow * R_flow / P_drive), and compare with 45 active and starburst galaxies from Fluetsch et al. (2019).
claims.result: BCG molecular flows are ~10-1000 times larger in extent (average ~12 kpc), ~10-100 times more massive, and have lifting factors two to three orders of magnitude higher than starbursts and quasar nuclei.
claims.finding: When active, radio-mechanical feedback is vastly more capable of lifting large molecular gas masses to higher altitudes per unit driving power than nuclear AGN winds and starbursts.

evidence.quote: The product of the molecular gas mass and lifting altitude divided by the AGN or starburst power — a parameter referred to as the lifting factor—exceeds starbursts and quasar nuclei by two to three orders of magnitude, respectively.

Figure [2](#thrust) shows BCGs have higher lifting factors on average than other outflow systems, indicating that radio-mechanical feedback is more effective per unit power at lifting large masses to greater distances than nuclear AGN and starbursts.

claims.hypothesis: AGN radiation pressure drives the molecular gas flows in BCGs.
claims.experiment: Compare molecular flow momentum flux (M_dot * v) to AGN radiative momentum flux (L_AGN / c) derived from nuclear X-ray luminosities.
claims.result: BCGs show no correlation between flow momentum flux and AGN radiative momentum flux (Pearson r = 0.24), and flow momentum rates exceed L_AGN/c by >= 20 in all BCGs except Phoenix.
claims.finding: Radiation pressure has little influence on driving molecular gas flows in BCGs; radio bubbles/mechanical power do the work.

evidence.quote: As expected, BCGs show no correlation between the flow momentum flux and the AGN radiative momentum flux (Pearson r-value of 0.24, the 50 percent confidence level). This lack of correlation suggests that radiation pressure has little influence on flows in BCGs.
In BCGs, the rate of change of flow momentum exceeds the radiative momentum input by $\ge 20$, more than the maximum theoretical prediction for energy conserving flows.

claims.hypothesis: Star formation is suppressed in BCGs relative to other active and starburst galaxies per unit molecular gas mass.
claims.experiment: Fit linear regressions to log(SFR) vs log(M_tot) for BCGs and Fluetsch galaxies, perform a two-sample t-test on the regression parameters, and compare surface densities with the Kennicutt-Schmidt law.
claims.result: BCGs have a lower SFR per unit molecular gas mass (five to ten times lower than the most massive AGN/starburst systems), with significantly different regression slopes (1.13 vs 1.66, t = 5.6, p < 0.005), though BCGs follow the normal Kennicutt-Schmidt relation while Fluetsch galaxies lie systematically above it.
claims.finding: Star formation per gram of molecular gas is tentatively suppressed in BCGs relative to the Fluetsch active galaxies, possibly because BCG gas resides in disordered off-nuclear filaments rather than circumnuclear disks, though selection bias cannot be ruled out.

evidence.quote: We find tentatively that star formation is suppressed in BCGs relative to other active galaxies, perhaps because these systems rarely form molecular disks that are more impervious to feedback and are better able to promote star formation.

evidence.loc: Does Radio-mode Feedback Suppress Star Formation?
evidence.quote: The observed difference between BCGs and Fluetsch galaxies in the relationship between their SFR and $M_{\rm tot}$ in log space is statistically significant. Given the small sample size, we cannot determine whether the separate trends are due to selection bias.
The star formation rate per gram of molecular gas in BCGs is five to ten times lower than the most massive systems with AGNs and starbursts studied by (cite: fluetsch18).

claims.hypothesis: Radio-mechanical feedback expels molecular gas permanently from BCGs.
claims.experiment: Compare observed molecular flow velocities in BCGs to escape velocities derived from a Hernquist gravitational potential model and integrate the CO spectrum beyond +/- v_esc.
claims.result: For all BCGs, molecular cloud velocities lie well below escape speeds and the escaped gas fraction is negligible.
claims.finding: Little or no molecular gas escapes the galaxy; instead, radio-mechanical feedback drives a fountain of gas that eventually returns to the central galaxy.

evidence.quote: We found that for all BCGs the escaped gas fraction is negligible.

Molecular cloud velocities in BCGs lie well below escape speeds. Similar to the systems in (cite: fluetsch18), little or no molecular gas is able to escape the galaxy. Radio-mechanical feedback is likely driving a fountain of hot and cold gas that eventually returns to the central galaxy.

why_this_data.value: ALMA provides unprecedented spatial and velocity resolution to resolve extended filamentary molecular gas flows in BCGs, which can be compared to the local active galaxy sample of Fluetsch et al. (2019) that omitted radio-mode feedback in central cluster galaxies.

evidence.quote: In recent years, the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) has observed molecular gas in central galaxies with unprecedented spatial and velocity resolution.

Here we analyze molecular flows in central galaxies and compare them to those in active galaxies from the (cite: fluetsch18) (Fluetsch). Fluetsch did not include outflows driven by radio-mode feedback in central galaxies.

why_this_method.value: Because BCG molecular flows are spatially resolved into off-nuclear filaments whose summed spectra may not deviate strongly from Gaussianity, flow properties are measured from spatially extended emission components rather than relying solely on broad spectral wings.

evidence.quote: Applying this method to Abell 2597, Abell 1835, AS1101 and NGC4696, the summed spectra deviate only marginally from gaussianity. Their flows would therefore have been missed were they too distant to be spatially resolved.
We identify gas flows in BCGs and determine their velocities and sizes individually from spatially extended emission components.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Spectroscopic 2-Gaussian broad-component method of Fluetsch et al. (2019) for flow speeds: tested for comparison, found to overestimate flow velocities by a factor of two and miss spatially resolved flows with nearly Gaussian summed spectra.

evidence.quote: Speeds estimated using the Fluetsch method are two times higher compared to our method, except for RXCJ0821.
The Fluetsch method captures a small fraction of the gas that is flowing at high speeds and overestimates the flow velocity. In what follows, we adopt speeds estimated using our method.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Including displaced hot X-ray atmospheric gas masses in flow rates and lifting factors: omitted in order to maintain a direct comparison of molecular gas phases with the Fluetsch sample.

evidence.quote: Therefore, in order to compare our systems with Fluetsch, we have not included the hot gas masses. But were we to do so the flow rates and masses would increase by a factor of two or more.

limitations_admitted.value: The BCG sample is biased and incomplete because targets were selected for ALMA observations based on having large molecular gas reservoirs.

evidence.quote: Most ALMA archival targets were observed based on their large molecular gas reservoirs (cite: edge02; pulido18). Therefore, our sample is biased, incomplete and does not represent all central cluster galaxies.

limitations_admitted.value: True flow sizes and velocities are systematically underestimated due to projection and orientation effects.

evidence.quote: The true sizes of molecular flows and their velocities are systematically underestimated due to projection.

limitations_admitted.value: In emission, it is unknown whether individual filaments are flowing outward or inward, and simultaneous inflows and outflows along the line of sight can lower observed flux-weighted velocities.

evidence.quote: Therefore, whether the filaments in an individual object are flowing in or out is unknown. Both inflows and outflows can be present at the same time.

limitations_admitted.value: The adopted CO-to-H2 conversion factor X_CO introduces a factor of two or more (0.3 dex) uncertainty in molecular gas mass estimates.

evidence.quote: The adopted value of $X_{\rm CO}$ lends to a factor of two or more uncertainty in the gas mass estimates.
The primary mass uncertainty comes from the application of $X_{\rm CO}$, which contributes 0.3 dex (cite: bolatto13).

limitations_admitted.value: Interferometric filtering by ALMA may resolve out 25 to 40 percent of extended molecular gas in some systems (A1664, A1835, NGC5044) compared to single-dish measurements.

evidence.quote: ALMA detected 60 percent more molecular gas in RXCJ0821, while in A1664, A1835 and NGC5044 the ALMA masses lie 25 to 40 percent below the single dish mass measurements. In the latter systems, ALMA may have resolved away some extended molecular gas.

limitations_admitted.value: Molecular gas surface densities may be overestimated by a factor of ~2 in some BCGs where the molecular gas is more extended than the UV star-forming region.

evidence.loc: Does Radio-mode Feedback Suppress Star Formation?
evidence.quote: In some BCGs (e.g., Abell S1101, RXCJ1539.5, PKS0745), molecular gas is more extended than the star forming region. Therefore, the molecular gas surface densities may be overestimated by a factor of $\sim$2 in these systems.

referee_caveats_inferred: The definition of 'flow' in BCGs treats all off-nuclear filamentary gas as a flow (and uses R_flow / v_flow as the flow timescale), whereas in the comparison sample of Fluetsch et al. (2019) outflows are defined kinematically from broad spectral wings; this methodological difference could systematically inflate BCG flow masses and lifting factors.

Appendices 1 and B (containing the exact flow region maps, velocity maps, and velocity adjustment tests) are referenced in the text but omitted from the main article body, making exact verification of the spatial masks difficult.
Sample count discrepancy between the Abstract/Summary/Table 1 (14 BCGs total, including NGC 1275 from IRAM and 13 ALMA targets) and Section 2 ('Archival ALMA observations of 12 BCGs were analyzed').

evidence.quote: The ALMA data used in this article is publicly available at [https://almascience.nrao.edu/aq/]( https://almascience.nrao.edu/aq/).

Specific CO transition and spectral window setup used per BCG
CLEAN imaging parameters (cell size, channel width, cleaning threshold, masks, beam size) and UVCONTSUB channel ranges for each target
Details of which targets were self-calibrated and with what parameters
Exact star-formation region areas measured from HST UV images for the eight BCGs
reproducibility.estimated_data_volume_inferred: Moderate (~50-200 GB of raw archival ALMA visibility data across 8 project codes for 13 BCGs, plus ~1-5 GB of reduced image cubes)
reproducibility.score_reason: All ALMA project codes are listed and public, CASA versions and weighting (Briggs robust=2) are stated, and the physical formulas, conversion factors, and per-target derived quantities (Table 1) are explicitly provided. However, target-level imaging parameters, continuum-subtraction channel ranges, and the exact spatial regions defining the filamentary flows (deferred to an appendix not included in the text) are missing.
reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: All archival ALMA datasets are public with project codes explicitly given, the analysis pipeline from CO cubes to flow masses, velocities, sizes, and scaling relations is straightforward, and Table 1 provides complete target-by-target numeric answer keys.
